sections.heading: What are the main types of seizure and what do they feel like?
sections.body:
Epilepsy seizures are grouped by where they start in the brain and how much of it is involved. Focal seizures start in one part of the brain, and some people stay aware during them while for others awareness is affected. Generalised seizures start in, or very quickly affect, both sides of the brain.

Some people notice a warning before a seizure, called an aura. Epilepsy Action says an aura is a type of focal seizure in its own right. Examples include a rising feeling in the tummy, unusual smells or tastes, and tingling in the arms and legs.

In a tonic-clonic seizure the person loses consciousness and the muscles go stiff, so someone who is standing may fall. This is followed by repeated jerking of the arms or legs. A seizure that begins on one side of the brain can also spread to both sides, which is called a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.

sections.heading: How is epilepsy diagnosed?
sections.body:
Epilepsy Action advises seeing a GP as soon as possible after a suspected seizure, even if the person did not go to hospital at the time. NICE says people with a suspected first seizure should be referred urgently so that a specialist is involved early in diagnosing epilepsy, and its quality standard aims for them to be seen within 2 weeks. Epilepsy Action says anyone with a suspected seizure should have an ECG, a heart tracing, to rule out a heart problem.

No single test can confirm epilepsy. An EEG may be requested, and if it is done after a first seizure it should be done as soon as possible. A normal EEG does not rule epilepsy out, because many people with epilepsy do not show abnormal activity between seizures. NHS inform says a diagnosis can still be made from the person's description of their seizures even when tests show nothing. NICE recommends an MRI scan for most people who are diagnosed with epilepsy. An MRI scan cannot decide on its own whether someone has epilepsy and is useful alongside other information.

Epilepsy Action advises keeping a seizure diary and taking it to appointments.

sections.heading: How is epilepsy treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says medicine to prevent seizures, called anti-seizure medicine, is the main treatment for epilepsy. NHS 111 Wales says these medicines help control seizures in about 7 out of 10 people. They do not cure epilepsy, but they can stop seizures happening. NHS inform says some anti-seizure medicines can reduce how well some types of contraception work. The NHS says it is very important to discuss treatment with a specialist if there is a chance of becoming pregnant while taking epilepsy medicine.

Other options are considered when medicines do not control the seizures. The NHS describes surgery as an option for rare cases. NICE's evidence review describes vagus nerve stimulation as used for people whose seizures have not responded to anti-seizure medicines and who are not suitable for surgery. The ketogenic diet, which is high in fat and low in carbohydrate and protein, is mainly used in children, usually those who have not responded to medicines. NHS inform says it should only be used under the supervision of an epilepsy specialist with the help of a dietitian.

sections.heading: What should happen if someone has a seizure?
sections.body:
NHS advice for a convulsive seizure is to cushion or gently hold the person's head to protect it from injury. Epilepsy Action adds that anything potentially harmful nearby should be cleared. The NHS also advises not restraining the person and not putting anything in their mouth. Once the jerking stops, the advice is to turn the person onto their side in the recovery position.

The NHS says to call 999 for an ambulance if it is the person's first seizure, if the seizure lasts longer than is usual for them, or if it lasts more than 5 minutes and their usual pattern is not known. A 999 call is also advised if the person does not recover as usual, has another seizure before recovering, is seriously injured or has trouble breathing. Status epilepticus, a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or seizures back to back with no recovery in between, needs emergency treatment, and NHS inform says to phone 999 straight away if it is suspected.

sections.heading: Living with epilepsy and the outlook
sections.body:
NHS 111 Wales suggests keeping a seizure diary, noting when seizures happen and what the person was doing beforehand, to help work out triggers. Epilepsy charities and NHS guidance list lack of sleep, missing anti-seizure medicine, stress and alcohol among possible triggers, and the CDC lists hormonal changes with a period. Flashing lights trigger seizures in a small number of people.

GOV.UK says a person must stop driving straight away after any epileptic seizure and tell the DVLA. When driving can start again depends on the type of seizure and how long the person has been seizure-free. Epilepsy can also affect decisions about contraception and planning a pregnancy.

The NHS says an epileptic seizure usually stops by itself and does not cause any lasting problems. Rarely, a seizure can last a long time, or several can happen without recovery in between, which is called status epilepticus and is a medical emergency that needs a 999 call. There is also a small risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). The NHS describes SUDEP as rare and says epilepsy treatment can reduce the risk. The CDC lists frequent or uncontrolled seizures among the factors linked to a higher risk. Epilepsy Action says there is not enough research to show that anti-suffocation pillows reduce the risk.

faqs.q: Can epilepsy be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says anti-seizure medicines do not cure epilepsy, but they can stop seizures happening. NHS 111 Wales says they help control seizures in about 7 out of 10 people. When medicines do not work well enough, other options such as surgery, nerve stimulation or a special diet may be discussed with an epilepsy specialist.

faqs.q: Does a normal EEG mean it is not epilepsy?
faqs.a: No. A normal EEG does not rule epilepsy out, because many people with epilepsy do not show abnormal activity between seizures. No single test can confirm epilepsy. Doctors weigh the EEG together with the story of what happened, any scan results and other information.

faqs.q: Can I drive after a seizure?
faqs.a: GOV.UK says a person must stop driving straight away after any epileptic seizure and tell the DVLA. When they can start again depends on the type of seizure and how long they have been seizure-free. The exception is for people who have already been given permission to drive with their type of seizures.

faqs.q: What is an aura?
faqs.a: An aura is a warning that some people have before a seizure. Epilepsy Action says it is a type of focal seizure in its own right. Examples include a rising feeling in the tummy, unusual smells or tastes, and tingling in the arms and legs.

faqs.q: When should I call 999 for a seizure?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 if it is the person's first seizure, if the seizure lasts longer than usual for them, or if it lasts more than 5 minutes and their usual pattern is not known. It also advises calling if the person does not recover as usual, has another seizure before recovering, is seriously injured or has trouble breathing.

sections.heading: What do the symptoms feel like, and how does Parkinson's progress?
sections.body: Parkinson's disease usually develops gradually, and the symptoms are mild at first. The NHS lists three main movement symptoms: tremor, slowed movement and muscle stiffness. The tremor is shaking that typically starts in a hand or arm and is most noticeable when the limb is at rest. Slowed movement is called bradykinesia, and it can lead to a small-stepped, shuffling walk. Slowed movement can make everyday tasks difficult. Stiffness, also called rigidity, can make movement and facial expression harder and sometimes causes painful cramps. The order in which symptoms develop and how severe they are differs for each person. Symptoms generally worsen over time, and the speed of progression varies widely between people.

sections.heading: What other symptoms can happen?
sections.body: Parkinson's also brings symptoms that are not about movement. The NHS and NHS inform list balance problems, a reduced sense of smell, nerve pain, bladder problems, constipation, sweating, swallowing difficulties, and changes in mood or memory. Balance problems can make a fall more likely, and a fall can lead to injury. A loss of the sense of smell sometimes occurs several years before other symptoms develop. The NHS also lists problems sleeping (insomnia) among the symptoms that are not about movement. NHS 111 Wales lists depression, anxiety and dementia among the cognitive and psychiatric symptoms. A review of advanced Parkinson's disease says that late-stage patients develop motor and non-motor complications that can greatly affect quality of life.

sections.heading: How is Parkinson's disease diagnosed?
sections.body: The NHS says that no test can conclusively show that someone has Parkinson's disease. A doctor bases the diagnosis on the symptoms, the medical history and a detailed physical examination. If Parkinson's is suspected, the GP refers the person to a specialist, such as a neurologist, for a formal diagnosis. Blood tests and brain scans may be used to rule out other conditions. A DaT scan is a brain scan, done in a nuclear medicine department, that looks at dopamine transporters in the brain. It can help tell Parkinson's apart from conditions such as essential tremor, and NICE recommends DaT scans only in selected cases. For the scan, a tracer is injected into a vein and the person lies still, and the report goes to the referring doctor, who contacts the person to discuss the results.

sections.heading: What treatments are used?
sections.body: There is currently no cure for Parkinson's disease, but treatments are available to help reduce the main symptoms and maintain quality of life. Treatment can include medicine, therapies such as physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy, and sometimes surgery. Most people with Parkinson's eventually need a medicine called levodopa. The NHS says levodopa usually improves movement problems. MAO-B inhibitors are another option in early Parkinson's disease and give less improvement in movement symptoms than levodopa. When tablets no longer give enough control, some people are considered for levodopa gel delivered through a tube into the small intestine. Another device-aided option is a continuous infusion of apomorphine under the skin. Deep brain stimulation is a type of surgery that does not cure Parkinson's disease but can ease symptoms for some people. It involves implanting a device, sometimes called a brain pacemaker, with leads placed in the brain by stereotactic surgery. It is considered for people whose symptoms are no longer well controlled by oral medicines.

sections.heading: Living with Parkinson's disease
sections.body: Regular exercise can help relieve muscle stiffness, lift mood and reduce stress. Many people with Parkinson's have problems with speech and swallowing. A speech and language therapist can often help by teaching speaking and swallowing exercises. An occupational therapist can pinpoint everyday tasks that are hard, such as dressing or getting to the shops. Occupational therapists can also provide equipment and strategies that help people stay independent and safe at home. A physiotherapist can work on muscle stiffness and joint pain through movement and exercise. Parkinson's nurse specialists can help arrange referrals to physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy. As the condition advances, it can become increasingly difficult to carry out everyday activities without help.

sections.heading: What is the outlook?
sections.body: NHS 111 Wales says that Parkinson's disease does not directly cause people to die, but it can leave them more vulnerable to serious infections. NHS 111 Wales says that most people with Parkinson's now have a normal or near-normal life expectancy. One single-centre study of hospital admissions found that respiratory infection was the most common cause, at 23% of admissions. A review of palliative care in advanced Parkinson's disease lists aspiration pneumonia, urinary tract infections, complications from falls and fractures, and sepsis from pressure ulcers as the main risks. A separate Rotterdam Study analysis found reduced life expectancy in people diagnosed with parkinsonism, mainly when diagnosis came before age 70. The outlook varies from person to person.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for Parkinson's disease?
faqs.a: There is currently no cure for Parkinson's disease. Treatments are available to help reduce the main symptoms and maintain quality of life, and they include medicine, physiotherapy and occupational therapy. For some people surgery called deep brain stimulation can ease symptoms, although it does not cure the condition.

faqs.q: Can a test confirm Parkinson's disease?
faqs.a: The NHS says that no test can conclusively show that someone has Parkinson's disease. A doctor bases the diagnosis on symptoms, medical history and a detailed examination. Blood tests and brain scans may be used to rule out other conditions, and a DaT scan, which looks at dopamine transporters in the brain, may be used when the diagnosis is unclear.

faqs.q: Does Parkinson's disease shorten life?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales says that most people with Parkinson's now have a normal or near-normal life expectancy. NHS 111 Wales says the condition does not directly cause death, but it can leave people more vulnerable to serious infections. A Rotterdam Study analysis found reduced life expectancy in people diagnosed with parkinsonism, mainly when diagnosis came before age 70.

faqs.q: Does Parkinson's disease only affect movement?
faqs.a: No, because people can also have balance problems, a reduced sense of smell, nerve pain, bladder problems, constipation, sweating, swallowing difficulties, and changes in mood or memory. The order in which symptoms develop and how severe they are differs for each person. A reduced sense of smell sometimes appears several years before other symptoms.

faqs.q: Who can help with everyday difficulties?
faqs.a: A physiotherapist can work on muscle stiffness and joint pain through movement and exercise. An occupational therapist can pinpoint everyday tasks that are hard, such as dressing or getting to the shops. A speech and language therapist can often help by teaching speaking and swallowing exercises. Parkinson's nurse specialists can help arrange referrals to these therapies.

sections.heading: How does Alzheimer's disease feel and progress?
sections.body: The NHS describes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease as becoming increasingly severe as the condition progresses. The Alzheimer's Society says memory loss is usually the first and main symptom in the early stage. The NHS lists trouble finding the right word and poorer judgement as early symptoms, and changes in mood can occur too. Early symptoms also include becoming less flexible and more hesitant to try new things. In the middle stage, existing memory and thinking problems get worse, and many people find it harder to recognise family or close friends. Confusion about time and place becomes more severe, some people develop delusions or hallucinations, and help with daily tasks increases. In the later stage, the NHS lists difficulty eating and swallowing, weight loss and incontinence, which means passing urine or stools unintentionally. NHS 111 Wales says that in the severe stages people may need full-time care and help with eating, moving and using the toilet.

sections.heading: What other types of dementia are there?
sections.body: Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia, and other common types include vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia. The Alzheimer's Society says around 19 in 20 people with dementia have one of four main types. When someone has more than one type it is called mixed dementia, and the most common mix is Alzheimer's disease with vascular dementia. The Alzheimer's Society says mixed dementia affects at least 1 in 10 people diagnosed with dementia. Young-onset dementia is dementia that begins before the age of 65. Younger people are less likely to have memory loss as one of their first symptoms, and they are more likely to have a rarer form such as frontotemporal dementia. Mild cognitive impairment is not a type of dementia, but people with it have an increased risk of developing dementia.

sections.heading: How is Alzheimer's disease assessed?
sections.body: For gradual memory problems, the GP is the usual first point of contact. A GP typically asks about symptoms, may examine the person and sets memory and thinking tasks. If the GP is unsure, the person may be referred to a specialist, such as an old age psychiatrist or a neurologist, who may be based in a memory clinic. Blood tests are mainly used to rule out other underlying causes rather than to make the diagnosis itself. According to NHS England, brain scans such as CT or MRI are not essential for a clinical diagnosis. A CT scan can check for signs of a stroke or a brain tumour, and shrinkage seen on a scan may support a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease but cannot point to a specific diagnosis. PET scans are typically used when earlier scans are unclear. There is no single test that confirms dementia, so assessment combines the history, memory and thinking tasks and sometimes scans.

sections.heading: What treatments and support are available?
sections.body: The NHS says there is no cure for Alzheimer's disease, but some medicines can temporarily ease symptoms or, for some people, slow progression. Donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine can be prescribed for early to mid-stage disease, and memantine is used for moderate or severe disease. Non-drug options include cognitive stimulation therapy, which uses group activities and exercises to build memory and problem-solving skills. The NHS describes cognitive rehabilitation as using the parts of the brain that are working to help the parts that are not. Reminiscence and life story work involves talking about things and events from the person's past. The NHS says coping strategies are tried first for aggression, and if they fail a consultant psychiatrist can prescribe risperidone for persistent aggression or extreme distress, using it for the shortest time possible because of its serious side effects. The Alzheimer's Society says lecanemab and donanemab are approved for use in the UK but not on the NHS. NICE's final draft guidance said their benefits remain too small to justify the additional costs to the NHS, so the NICE website has the current position.

sections.heading: Living with Alzheimer's disease and caring for someone
sections.body: NHS inform suggests keeping in touch with people and joining activities, and notes that dementia-friendly groups, communities, sport and cultural activities exist for people with dementia. It says a daily routine can encourage feelings of security, value and worth. Suggested memory aids around the home include pictures on cupboard doors showing what is inside, and technology such as a device that plays a recorded reminder when the front door is opened. Local councils provide information about aids and adaptations for the home, and memory services can offer memory aids and strategies. Depression is common in dementia, and NHS inform says a GP can talk through talking treatments that can help. A care needs assessment can be arranged through social services, and carers can ask the local council for a carer's assessment. NHS inform describes advance care planning as thinking ahead about which treatments a person would want, including whether they would want certain end-of-life treatments.

sections.heading: What are the complications and the outlook?
sections.body: The Alzheimer's Society says the middle stage of dementia is often the longest. In the later stage many people have trouble eating or swallowing, which can lead to choking, chest infections and other problems. Delirium is a sudden change in mental state, where the person seems not themselves, and it is different from the slow worsening of dementia. The Alzheimer's Society says dementia can make a person much more likely to have delirium. Urinary tract infections can cause sudden and severe confusion in someone with memory problems or dementia, and confusion can also be a sign of a stroke or sepsis. NHS services such as South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust advise going to A&E or calling 999 if someone suddenly becomes confused. The Alzheimer's Society advises making an urgent GP appointment or calling NHS 111 for a sudden change in someone with dementia. Once the cause is treated, symptoms usually improve within a few days for many people, though some have memory and thinking problems for longer.

faqs.q: Is Alzheimer's disease the same as dementia?
faqs.a: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, but it is not the only one. The Alzheimer's Society says around 19 in 20 people with dementia have one of four main types. Some people have more than one type, which is called mixed dementia, and the most common mix is Alzheimer's disease with vascular dementia. Young-onset dementia is dementia that begins before the age of 65.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for Alzheimer's disease?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure, but some medicines can temporarily ease symptoms or, for some people, slow progression. Non-drug approaches such as cognitive stimulation therapy and reminiscence work are also used. A care needs assessment can be arranged through social services, and carers can ask the local council for a carer's assessment.

faqs.q: Will I need a brain scan?
faqs.a: According to NHS England, brain scans such as CT or MRI are not essential for a clinical diagnosis. A CT scan can check for signs of a stroke or a brain tumour, and shrinkage seen on a scan may support a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease. PET scans are typically used when earlier scans are unclear.

faqs.q: Why might someone with dementia suddenly become much more confused?
faqs.a: A sudden change is different from the slow worsening of dementia and may be delirium. Urinary tract infections are one cause of sudden and severe confusion in someone with dementia. NHS services advise going to A&E or calling 999 for sudden confusion, and the Alzheimer's Society advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for a sudden change in someone with dementia.

faqs.q: Do memory problems always mean dementia?
faqs.a: Memory problems are not always caused by dementia, so the GP may look for other causes. A GP typically asks about symptoms, may examine the person and sets memory and thinking tasks. Blood tests are mainly used to rule out other underlying causes rather than to make the diagnosis itself. If the GP is unsure, the person may be referred to a specialist, who may be based in a memory clinic.

sections.heading: How does chronic kidney disease feel and progress?
sections.body:
Early chronic kidney disease usually causes no symptoms, and it is often found by chance when a blood or urine test is done for another reason. Symptoms can appear at a more advanced stage, including tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands, shortness of breath, feeling sick and blood in the urine. Later kidney failure can also bring itching and muscle cramps.

Doctors describe the condition in stages, and a higher stage means more severe disease. In stage 1 the filtering is normal but there is other evidence of kidney damage, and stage 2 is a slight decrease in function. Stage 3 is split into 3a and 3b, and stage 5 is kidney failure. Only a small proportion of people with the condition go on to kidney failure, which the NHS puts at around 2 in 100 people. When the kidneys do stop working, this usually happens slowly.

sections.heading: How is it checked?
sections.body:
Chronic kidney disease can be diagnosed with blood and urine tests. The blood test is used to estimate how well the kidneys are filtering, and the urine test looks for protein and blood. One abnormal result is not usually enough, and repeated tests are used to confirm the diagnosis. The blood test result, called the eGFR, is used to give a stage from 1 to 5.

In many cases the condition is only found when a routine blood or urine test, done for another problem, shows that the kidneys may not be working normally. NHS guidance lists high blood pressure, diabetes and heart disease as reasons for regular testing. The NHS says most people with the condition can control it with medicine and regular check-ups.

sections.heading: What treatments are used?
sections.body:
There is no cure for chronic kidney disease, but treatment can help relieve the symptoms and stop it getting worse. The NHS describes lifestyle changes to stay as healthy as possible, together with medicines to manage problems such as high blood pressure and high cholesterol. ACE inhibitors are often used for blood pressure in this condition, and statins are prescribed to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, meaning heart and blood vessel problems.

Anaemia, a shortage of red blood cells, can develop in kidney disease, and the NHS says tablets or injections may be given to help the body make more red blood cells. Medical reviews describe anaemia in kidney disease as traditionally treated with iron preparations or erythropoiesis-stimulating agents. Medicines can also be used for other symptoms of kidney failure, such as breathlessness, loss of appetite and itchy skin.

sections.heading: What are dialysis and a kidney transplant?
sections.body:
For a small number of people the kidneys eventually stop working, and dialysis or a transplant is then considered. Dialysis is a way of removing waste products and extra fluid from the blood. NIDDK describes haemodialysis as a machine filtering the blood outside the body, while peritoneal dialysis uses the lining of the abdomen to filter waste and extra fluid.

A kidney transplant is the other main option, and the kidney can come from a living or a deceased donor. NHS Blood and Transplant says living donors account for roughly 30 in 100 kidney transplants, with a much shorter wait than for a kidney from a deceased donor. People with a transplant take anti-rejection medicines, and NIDDK notes these can cause other health problems. Some people choose not to have dialysis or a transplant, and conservative care then continues their care without either, including treatment for symptoms.

sections.heading: Living with chronic kidney disease
sections.body:
A hospital leaflet from an NHS trust says that with good care many people with chronic kidney disease live long and active lives. It favours plenty of fruit and vegetables, including pulses, with smaller amounts of animal protein such as meat, fish and eggs. Kidney Care UK says a diet low in salt and rich in fibre and potassium from fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts, seeds and pulses helps to lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of complications.

Kidney Care UK also notes that studies have shown exercise can improve kidney function. NHS 111 Wales lists some long-term medicines, including NSAIDs and lithium, among the causes of chronic kidney disease. The hospital leaflet says over-the-counter anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are avoided unless a medical professional advises otherwise, because these medicines can harm the kidneys in people with kidney disease.

sections.heading: Complications and outlook
sections.body:
Heart and blood vessel disease is a major concern in chronic kidney disease. One review says cardiovascular complications are the most common cause of death in people with kidney failure on regular dialysis, and that most people with progressive chronic kidney disease die before reaching kidney failure because of the high rate of cardiovascular death.

Many people with stage 3, 4 and 5 disease develop anaemia. Mineral and bone disorder can also develop in advanced kidney disease and is linked to a higher risk of bone fractures, heart and blood vessel events and death. NHS 111 Wales gives the proportion of people with the condition who reach kidney failure as around 1 in 50.

faqs.q: Can chronic kidney disease be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure for chronic kidney disease, but treatment can help relieve symptoms and stop it getting worse. The NHS says most people can control the condition with medicine and regular check-ups. A hospital leaflet from an NHS trust adds that with good care many people live long and active lives.

faqs.q: Does it always lead to kidney failure?
faqs.a: No, only a small proportion of people do. The NHS says around 2 in 100 people with the condition reach kidney failure, and NHS 111 Wales gives the figure as around 1 in 50. When the kidneys do stop working, this usually happens slowly rather than suddenly.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the two kinds of dialysis?
faqs.a: Dialysis removes waste products and extra fluid from the blood. In haemodialysis, a machine filters the blood outside the body. In peritoneal dialysis, the lining of the abdomen is used to filter waste and extra fluid. NIDDK describes a kidney transplant and conservative management as the other treatment paths for kidney failure.

faqs.q: Does everyone with kidney failure have dialysis or a transplant?
faqs.a: No. NIDDK describes conservative management as continuing a person's care without dialysis or a kidney transplant. The NHS says medicines can be used to treat symptoms of kidney failure such as breathlessness, loss of appetite and itchy skin, as part of supportive care.

faqs.q: Which painkillers can affect the kidneys?
faqs.a: A hospital leaflet from an NHS trust says over-the-counter anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen can harm the kidneys in people with kidney disease and are avoided unless a medical professional advises otherwise. NHS 111 Wales also lists long-term use of some medicines, including NSAIDs and lithium, among the causes of chronic kidney disease.

faqs.q: Does diet matter in chronic kidney disease?
faqs.a: A hospital leaflet from an NHS trust favours plenty of fruit and vegetables, including pulses, with smaller amounts of animal protein such as meat, fish and eggs. Kidney Care UK describes a diet low in salt and rich in fibre and potassium from fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts, seeds and pulses as helping to lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of complications.

sections.heading: What does anaemia feel like?
sections.body:
Many people with iron deficiency anaemia have only a few symptoms. How much a person notices depends on how quickly the anaemia develops, and iron deficiency can be mild enough to cause no symptoms. Tiredness and a lack of energy are common, and some people also notice shortness of breath, a pounding heartbeat, paler skin or headaches. Less often there may be ringing in the ears, an altered sense of taste, hair loss, a craving to eat non-food items (called pica) or spoon-shaped nails. Low iron has also been linked with restless legs syndrome, even when anaemia is not fully present.

Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia can cause tiredness, a sore red tongue, pins and needles and mouth ulcers. It can also cause muscle weakness and problems with vision, memory or judgement. Some of these problems, especially those affecting the nervous system, can become permanent without treatment, and long-term B12 deficiency can damage nerves. The NHS says body stores of B12 can last for a few years, so problems may take a long time to appear.

sections.heading: What are the main types of anaemia?
sections.body:
Iron deficiency is the most common type of anaemia, and vitamin B12 and folate deficiency can also cause it. MedlinePlus also lists anaemia of chronic disease, sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia and aplastic anaemia among the types. Anaemia of chronic disease is linked with long-term illnesses. Sickle cell anaemia is inherited and involves abnormal haemoglobin that changes the shape of red blood cells. Thalassaemia is inherited, while aplastic anaemia involves damage to the stem cells in the bone marrow that make blood cells.

In the UK, the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency is pernicious anaemia. In this condition the immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach, so the body cannot absorb B12 from food. Diet can also contribute, particularly for people who eat little or no animal-source food, such as vegans, and some medicines, including anticonvulsants and proton pump inhibitors, can reduce absorption. Folate deficiency can also follow alcohol misuse.

sections.heading: What happens at an appointment, and which tests are used?
sections.body:
A GP usually asks about lifestyle and medical history and then arranges a blood test. This is a full blood count, which checks the red blood cells, and the GP may also test ferritin, a protein that stores iron. A low ferritin suggests that there is not much iron stored in the body. The NHS advises seeing a GP if iron deficiency anaemia is suspected, and diagnosis relies on blood tests.

Finding the cause matters because treatment depends on it. Heavy periods and medicines such as ibuprofen or aspirin, which can cause bleeding in the stomach, are among the causes the GP considers. In men and in women after the menopause, bleeding in the gut is the most common cause of iron deficiency, whereas in women before the menopause it is heavy periods. If the cause is unclear, further tests may follow, such as a gastroscopy or colonoscopy to look for a source of bleeding, and testing for coeliac disease may be suggested.

sections.heading: How is anaemia treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on the type of anaemia and its cause. Iron deficiency anaemia is usually treated with iron tablets and iron-rich foods, while the underlying cause, such as heavy periods or bleeding, is also addressed. Common side effects of iron tablets include constipation or diarrhoea, tummy pain, heartburn, feeling sick and darker than usual poo. Taking tablets with or shortly after food can help, and a GP may adjust the tablets if side effects are troublesome. An iron infusion may be used when a person cannot take tablets or cannot absorb iron through the gut.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is usually treated with hydroxocobalamin injections, followed by tablets or continuing injections depending on the cause. When the deficiency is not caused by diet, injections may be needed long term. Folate deficiency is treated with folic acid tablets, and doctors check B12 first because folic acid can sometimes hide a B12 deficiency. After iron treatment, a follow-up blood test is used to check the response. MedlinePlus says anaemia of chronic disease may improve when the disease causing it is treated.

sections.heading: Living with anaemia and what to expect
sections.body:
Vitamin B12 is found in meat, fish, eggs, dairy products and fortified foods. Good sources of folate include broccoli, brussels sprouts, asparagus, peas, chickpeas and brown rice. NHS 111 Wales notes that an iron overdose in a young child can be fatal, which is why iron tablets are kept out of children's reach.

NHS 111 Wales says most people with iron deficiency anaemia respond to dietary changes and iron tablets. Untreated iron deficiency anaemia may lead to heart problems, complications in pregnancy and delayed development in children. Delays in treating B12 deficiency can cause lasting nerve damage. Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia most often responds well to treatment. Overall, the outlook depends on the condition causing the anaemia.

faqs.q: Is anaemia the same as iron deficiency?
faqs.a: No, iron deficiency is only the most common type. Anaemia can also come from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, long-term conditions, inherited conditions such as sickle cell disease and thalassaemia, or aplastic anaemia. Treatment depends on the type and cause.

faqs.q: Why do doctors look for the cause of iron deficiency?
faqs.a: Finding the cause matters because treatment depends on it. In men and in women after the menopause, bleeding in the gut is the most common cause. Doctors may arrange a gastroscopy or colonoscopy to look for a source of bleeding, including a cancer, if the reason is unclear.

faqs.q: Do iron tablets have side effects?
faqs.a: They can, and the NHS lists constipation or diarrhoea, tummy pain, heartburn, feeling sick and darker than usual poo. Taking them with or shortly after food can help. A GP may adjust the tablets if the side effects are troublesome. An iron infusion may be used when a person cannot take tablets or cannot absorb iron through the gut.

faqs.q: Why might vitamin B12 be given by injection?
faqs.a: Injections are used when the problem is poor absorption, as in pernicious anaemia, where the immune system attacks healthy stomach cells. The NHS says vitamin B12 injections are called hydroxocobalamin. When low B12 is only due to diet, tablets may be enough.

faqs.q: Does anaemia always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No, many people with iron deficiency anaemia have only a few symptoms. Sources note that iron deficiency can be mild enough to cause no symptoms, so a blood test is the reliable way to confirm it. The NHS advises seeing a GP for anyone who thinks they may have iron deficiency anaemia.

sections.heading: What does an underactive thyroid feel like?
sections.body:
An underactive thyroid develops slowly, and symptoms may not show for months or even years. Because the changes build up gradually, some people go months or even years without noticing symptoms. The NHS lists common symptoms such as feeling very tired, putting on weight, feeling colder than usual and constipation. A croaky or hoarse voice is also described, and some women have heavy or irregular periods. Symptoms often resemble those of other conditions, which can delay recognition.

Many of these problems have other explanations, so a blood test that measures hormone levels is the only accurate way to confirm a thyroid problem. The NHS describes an underactive thyroid as usually lifelong, and says it can be managed with medicine.

sections.heading: What causes an underactive thyroid?
sections.body:
The main cause in the UK is Hashimoto's disease, which is an autoimmune condition. Autoimmune means the body's defence system mistakenly attacks its own tissue, in this case the thyroid. Inflammation of the thyroid, called thyroiditis, is another cause. Not getting enough iodine in the diet can also be a cause, but the NHS says this is rare in the UK.

Surgery or radiotherapy around the neck or thyroid can also lead to it. Treatment for an overactive thyroid can lead to it as well. The NIDDK says people who receive radioactive iodine treatment will probably eventually develop an underactive thyroid. Certain medicines, including lithium, amiodarone and interferon alpha, have been linked to the condition. Some babies are born with an underactive thyroid, which is called congenital hypothyroidism.

sections.heading: What happens at an appointment, and which tests are used?
sections.body:
A GP may ask about symptoms and may feel the neck to check whether the thyroid is enlarged. The TSH blood test needs no special preparation, according to MedlinePlus. MedlinePlus also says biotin (vitamin B7) can distort TSH results. TSH is a hormone made by the pituitary gland that tells the thyroid how much to produce. A high level of TSH together with a low level of thyroid hormone (T4) can point to an underactive thyroid.

When Hashimoto's disease is suspected, a blood test for thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies can be used, and the NIDDK says it is positive in most people with the condition. An ultrasound scan may be used if antibodies are not found but Hashimoto's disease is still suspected. The NIDDK says ultrasound can also help rule out other causes of an enlarged thyroid, such as nodules. The NIDDK adds that further testing is usually unnecessary to confirm the diagnosis.

sections.heading: How is an underactive thyroid treated?
sections.body:
The usual treatment is levothyroxine tablets. Levothyroxine replaces the thyroid hormone the body is missing. NHS inform says people usually need to take it for the rest of their lives. Some people with very mild symptoms, or none, may not need any treatment.

Regular blood tests are used at the start until the right dose is found. A follow-up blood test is usually arranged after a dose is started or changed. The NIDDK says the condition can most likely be controlled with thyroid hormone medicine as long as the recommended dose is taken as instructed. The NIDDK also warns that taking too much thyroid hormone medicine can cause serious problems, such as atrial fibrillation (an irregular heart rhythm) or osteoporosis (weak bones). NHS guidance says the wrong dose can cause side effects such as feeling sick, diarrhoea, headaches or problems sleeping.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, babies and children
sections.body:
The NHS advises telling the GP when pregnant or trying to conceive with an underactive thyroid. Further tests are needed, and the levothyroxine dose will probably change during pregnancy. Untreated, an underactive thyroid in pregnancy can raise the chance of problems such as pre-eclampsia, birth defects, premature birth or miscarriage.

Congenital hypothyroidism, an underactive thyroid present from birth, often has subtle signs or none at birth. This is why newborn screening matters. A clinical review reports that growth and development return to normal with early and adequate treatment. Some babies have a temporary form of the condition. Another review says some children treated early still have mild hearing deficits, so hearing should be checked periodically.

sections.heading: What are the complications and the outlook?
sections.body:
NHS 111 Wales says an underactive thyroid is not usually serious if the right treatment is being given. Untreated, it raises the risk of cardiovascular disease, according to the NHS, and NHS 111 Wales lists bone problems including osteoporosis. The NHS also lists goitre, which is an enlarged thyroid gland, and problems in pregnancy as possible complications.

A cardiology review describes the heart effects as typically reversible with hormone replacement. Myxoedema coma is a very rare but life-threatening complication that needs emergency hospital treatment. The route to care for myxoedema coma is to call 999. The NHS says treatment usually involves thyroid hormone replacement medicine given directly into a vein.

faqs.q: Is an underactive thyroid permanent?
faqs.a: NHS inform says people usually need to take levothyroxine for the rest of their lives. Regular blood tests are used at the start to find the right dose. Some people with very mild or no symptoms may not need treatment. The NIDDK says it can most likely be controlled with thyroid hormone medicine taken as instructed.

faqs.q: What is Hashimoto's disease?
faqs.a: Hashimoto's disease is an autoimmune condition in which the body's defence system attacks the thyroid. It is the main cause of an underactive thyroid in the UK, according to the NHS. The NHS says it is most common in women and usually starts between the ages of 30 and 50. A blood test for TPO antibodies can be part of the check, and the NIDDK says it is positive in most people with the condition.

faqs.q: How do doctors confirm an underactive thyroid?
faqs.a: A GP may ask about symptoms and may feel the neck to check whether the thyroid is enlarged. A blood test measuring hormone levels is the only accurate way to confirm a thyroid problem. A high TSH with a low T4 can point to an underactive thyroid.

faqs.q: Can an underactive thyroid affect pregnancy?
faqs.a: Untreated, it can raise the chance of problems such as pre-eclampsia, premature birth or miscarriage. The NHS advises telling the GP when pregnant or trying to conceive. Extra tests are then needed, and the levothyroxine dose will probably change during pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can an underactive thyroid be dangerous?
faqs.a: It is not usually serious with the right treatment, according to the NHS. Untreated, it can raise the risk of cardiovascular disease and of bone problems such as osteoporosis. Myxoedema coma is very rare but life-threatening and needs emergency hospital treatment, and the route to care is 999.

sections.heading: What does an overactive thyroid feel like?
sections.body:
The symptoms of an overactive thyroid can appear gradually or suddenly, and they vary in how severe they are. People often notice nervousness, irritability, mood swings, poor sleep and persistent tiredness. Other changes include sensitivity to heat and a tremor. Some people also have swelling in the neck from an enlarged thyroid gland, called a goitre. Because many of these symptoms can have other causes, symptoms alone cannot confirm the diagnosis.

In older adults the picture can look different, with loss of appetite and apathy rather than restlessness. For this reason the condition can be mistaken for depression or dementia in older people. The NHS advises seeing a GP for symptoms or signs of an overactive thyroid. A blood test of thyroid function is the usual first step.

sections.heading: What causes an overactive thyroid?
sections.body:
The most common cause is Graves' disease, an autoimmune condition. The NHS says about 4 in every 5 people with an overactive thyroid have Graves' disease. Other causes include thyroid nodules and inflammation of the gland called thyroiditis. The NHS says too much iodine, for example from medicines that contain it such as amiodarone, can also trigger an overactive thyroid. The NHS describes thyroiditis as swelling of the thyroid, which can cause extra thyroid hormones to be produced. A recent iodine load, such as from amiodarone or contrast dye, can make an uptake scan unreliable, so an antibody test may be used instead.

Further tests can help to tell the causes apart. An antibody blood test can help identify Graves' disease. A radioactive iodine uptake scan can also help, with high uptake typical of Graves' disease and low uptake typical of thyroiditis.

sections.heading: How is an overactive thyroid diagnosed?
sections.body: The starting point is a visit to a GP, who may arrange a thyroid function blood test. A diagnosis is based on the symptoms and the results of blood tests that assess how well the thyroid is working. These tests measure thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and the thyroid hormones T3 and T4. A low TSH with a high T3 or T4 usually points to an overactive thyroid. A mild form with a low TSH but normal T3 and T4 is called subclinical hyperthyroidism. Thyroid UK says many cases settle by themselves, so regular TSH checks are needed. Thyroid UK also says an undetectable TSH carries a higher risk of progressing to overt hyperthyroidism. Other blood tests and a thyroid uptake scan may be used to find the cause.

sections.heading: What are the treatments for an overactive thyroid?
sections.body:
The NHS describes three main treatments: medicine, radioactive iodine treatment and surgery. Antithyroid medicines such as carbimazole and propylthiouracil are a common first choice. They are usually taken for more than a year, and the medicine is then stopped to see whether the condition returns. Some people need to continue the medicine for several years or possibly for life. Beta-blockers, such as propranolol or atenolol, can relieve symptoms such as tremor and a rapid heartbeat, but they are not suitable for people with asthma.

Radioactive iodine is a highly effective treatment, and often a single dose is enough. It is not suitable for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, or for people with severe eye problems caused by the condition. Surgery is reserved for cases such as a large goitre, severe eye problems, when other treatments cannot be used, or when symptoms return. Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid, which is sometimes temporary but often permanent and needs long-term thyroid hormone medicine.

sections.heading: Can an overactive thyroid affect the eyes?
sections.body:
Eye problems, known as thyroid eye disease or Graves' ophthalmopathy, can occur in people whose overactive thyroid is caused by Graves' disease. NHS pages give different figures, from around 1 in 20 to around 1 in 4 people with Graves' disease. Symptoms can include dry and gritty eyes, red eyes, sensitivity to light, watering, blurred or double vision, and bulging eyes. Severe disease can cause vision loss, and treatments named by NHS inform include eye drops, sunglasses, corticosteroids, radiotherapy and surgery. Smoking increases the risk of thyroid eye disease, and quitting helps. Thyroid UK says eye problems can continue in people who keep smoking after their thyroid is treated.

An NHS hospital leaflet advises getting urgent advice from a doctor if the eyes become more prominent and swollen, for example from the GP the same day or NHS 111.

sections.heading: What about pregnancy?
sections.body: NIDDK says a woman with mild hyperthyroidism in pregnancy probably will not need treatment. Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism in pregnancy can lead to serious problems for the mother and the baby, according to NIDDK. NIDDK says more severe cases are typically treated with antithyroid medicines, most often propylthiouracil early in pregnancy. Radioactive iodine is not suitable during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and NIDDK says it can damage the baby's thyroid gland. NHS inform says becoming pregnant can lead to a relapse of symptoms, especially in someone with a history of Graves' disease. A UK hospital trust guideline suggests ultrasound scans in later pregnancy to watch the baby's growth when the mother has hyperthyroidism. Antibodies from a mother with Graves' disease can cross the placenta and affect the baby's thyroid function, according to a systematic review.

sections.heading: What are the complications and outlook?
sections.body: An overactive thyroid is usually treatable, according to the NHS. The NHS says an overactive thyroid can raise the risk of atrial fibrillation, heart failure and osteoporosis, which weakens the bones. Atrial fibrillation is an irregular and often abnormally fast heart rhythm. Rarely, an undiagnosed or poorly controlled overactive thyroid can lead to thyroid storm, a serious, life-threatening condition. The NHS lists triggers such as infection, pregnancy, missed doses of medicine and physical damage to the thyroid. Warning signs include a rapid heartbeat, high temperature, confusion and loss of consciousness. Severe thyroid eye disease can lead to vision loss, and radioactive iodine can leave the thyroid underactive. Thyroid storm is an emergency, and anyone with these signs needs 999.

faqs.q: Can an overactive thyroid get better without treatment?
faqs.a: A mild form with a low TSH but normal hormone levels, called subclinical hyperthyroidism, is often monitored with regular TSH checks, and Thyroid UK says many cases settle by themselves. Other people are treated with medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery. Some need medicine for several years or possibly for life. A GP can arrange the thyroid blood test that starts the process.

faqs.q: Is an overactive thyroid the same as an underactive thyroid?
faqs.a: No, an overactive thyroid makes too much thyroid hormone, while an underactive thyroid means hormone levels are too low. Radioactive iodine treatment for an overactive thyroid often leads to an underactive thyroid, which is sometimes temporary but often permanent. A permanent underactive thyroid needs long-term thyroid hormone medicine.

faqs.q: When is an overactive thyroid an emergency?
faqs.a: Thyroid storm is rare but life-threatening, and can occur when an overactive thyroid is undiagnosed or poorly controlled. Its signs include a rapid heartbeat, high temperature, confusion and loss of consciousness. Anyone with these signs needs an emergency response, so call 999.

faqs.q: Who cannot have radioactive iodine treatment?
faqs.a: NHS hospital guidance says radioactive iodine is not suitable in pregnancy or breastfeeding. It is also not suitable where eye disease is severe. Surgery is reserved for cases such as a large goitre, severe eye problems, when other treatments cannot be used, or when symptoms return.

faqs.q: Can an overactive thyroid be mistaken for something else?
faqs.a: Yes, many of its symptoms can have other causes, so symptoms alone cannot confirm it. In older adults it can be mistaken for depression or dementia. The symptoms can appear gradually or suddenly and vary in how severe they are. A thyroid function blood test helps to show whether a thyroid problem is responsible.

sections.heading: What does a gout flare feel like?
sections.body:
Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by urate crystals in and around joints, and it causes sudden flares of severe pain and swelling. The big toe is the most common site, and the ankles, knees, hands and fingers can also be affected. Left untreated, an attack usually lasts about one to two weeks. If gout is not treated, future attacks may last even longer.

Further flares are common. StatPearls reports that around six in ten people have a second attack within a year, and the NHS notes that flares can come back every few months or after years. Without treatment, attacks tend to come more often and can affect more joints. Hard lumps of urate called tophi can also form under the skin, usually around the ears, fingers and elbows.

sections.heading: How is gout diagnosed?
sections.body:
A blood test for uric acid may be done, but the level in the blood often falls during a flare. Because of this, the test may be repeated some weeks after the flare has settled. A normal result during a flare does not rule gout out, and a raised urate level on its own, without joint symptoms, is not a diagnosis of gout.

When the diagnosis is uncertain, fluid can be taken from the joint and looked at under a microscope for crystals, which is regarded as the reference standard. The fluid can also be tested for infection, because gout and septic arthritis can occur together. An ultrasound or a special CT scan can also check for crystal build-up in the joint if fluid cannot be taken or the diagnosis is still unclear.

sections.heading: How is a gout flare treated?
sections.body:
Treatment has two parts: easing a flare, and preventing future flares. NICE recommends an NSAID (an anti-inflammatory painkiller), colchicine or a short course of steroid tablets as first-line treatment for a flare, depending on the person's other conditions, medicines and preferences. NICE found no strong evidence that any one of these works better than the others when used first.

A steroid injection into the joint or a muscle is considered if NSAIDs and colchicine cannot be used, are not tolerated or do not work. NIAMS notes that colchicine works best when started as soon as symptoms appear. NHS medicines information says it can take a day or two before pain and inflammation start to get better with colchicine. Ice packs can also ease symptoms, according to NHS inform.

sections.heading: How are future flares prevented?
sections.body:
NICE describes gout as a lifelong condition that benefits from long-term urate-lowering treatment, which aims to clear the urate crystals and prevent flares. NICE says this treatment can also shrink tophi. NIAMS says a main goal of treatment is to prevent and resolve tophi so that joint damage stops.

Flares can increase when urate-lowering medicine is first started, so doctors may give another medicine alongside it for the first months. NICE recommends starting allopurinol low and increasing it slowly according to blood urate measurements. NIAMS says lifestyle changes alone are not enough when flares are frequent or tophi are present, so medicine is the main approach. The NHS says lifestyle changes can still help reduce future flares.

sections.heading: What diet and lifestyle changes help?
sections.body:
Versus Arthritis says heavy drinking, especially of beer and spirits, can raise urate levels and trigger attacks. It says beer is particularly bad because it contains a lot of purines, and that small amounts of wine do not appear to raise the risk. It advises losing weight gradually, and says extreme weight loss or starvation diets are not recommended because they can raise urate levels. The NHS also advises avoiding crash diets and lists dehydration as a possible trigger of an attack.

An NHS dietetic leaflet says regularly drinking sugar-sweetened drinks can increase the risk of gout, while sugar-free fizzy drinks do not. Versus Arthritis lists a daily glass of skimmed milk among its management tips. NHS inform notes that vitamin C supplements are not suitable for everyone and recommends talking to a GP before using them.

sections.heading: What are the complications and the outlook?
sections.body:
Leaving gout untreated may cause lasting damage to the joints, and the NHS notes that repeated attacks can damage joints and cause kidney stones. Severe gout pain can lead to feelings of depression or anxiety, according to NHS inform.

The NHS advises a GP appointment for a first episode of gout symptoms, or when usual treatments are not helping. For a painful swollen joint that is getting worse, especially with a very high temperature, feeling hot or shivery, or feeling sick or unable to eat, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111. These can be signs of an infection inside the joint, called septic arthritis. Gout can look the same as septic arthritis, which is why fluid from the joint may be tested for infection.

faqs.q: How long does a gout attack last?
faqs.a: Left untreated, a gout attack usually lasts about one to two weeks, and later attacks may last even longer. The NHS notes that flares can come back every few months or after years. NHS medicines information says colchicine can take a day or two before pain and inflammation start to get better.

faqs.q: Does gout go away on its own?
faqs.a: Without treatment, a flare usually lasts about one to two weeks, according to the NHS, but further flares are common. StatPearls reports that around six in ten people have a second attack within a year. NICE describes gout as a lifelong condition that benefits from long-term urate-lowering treatment to prevent flares. The NHS advises seeing a GP when usual treatments are not helping.

faqs.q: Should I have a uric acid blood test during a flare?
faqs.a: The level of urate in the blood often falls during a flare, so a test then can be misleading. The test may be repeated some weeks after the flare has settled. A normal result during a flare does not rule gout out, and a raised level on its own, without joint symptoms, is not a diagnosis of gout.

faqs.q: Is beer worse than wine for gout?
faqs.a: Versus Arthritis says heavy drinking, especially of beer and spirits, can raise urate levels and trigger attacks. It says beer is particularly bad because it contains a lot of purines, while small amounts of wine do not appear to raise the risk. An Oxford Kidney Unit leaflet advises people prone to gout attacks to reduce alcohol to a minimum or avoid it.

faqs.q: When should I get urgent help for a swollen joint?
faqs.a: For a painful swollen joint that is getting worse, especially with a very high temperature or feeling sick or unable to eat, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111. These can be signs of an infection inside the joint, called septic arthritis. The NHS advises a GP appointment for a first episode of gout symptoms.

keyFacts.value: Usually about one to two weeks if untreated

keyFacts.label: Usual joints
keyFacts.value: Big toe most often; also ankles, knees, hands and fingers

keyFacts.label: Flare treatment aims
keyFacts.value: Ease the flare with an NSAID, colchicine or steroids

keyFacts.label: Long-term treatment
keyFacts.value: Urate-lowering medicine for a lifelong condition

keyFacts.value: Urate can read normal in a flare, so the test may be repeated some weeks later
